newClaim.claimText: Princeton's Rights, Rules, Responsibilities (2.4) states that generative AI is not a source; where an instructor permits generative AI, students must disclose its use rather than cite or acknowledge it. Disclosure of permitted use is therefore required, not merely recommended, while whether AI may be used at all is set by the course or department. Scholarly Integrity guidance says failure to disclose, even in a course where AI is permitted, is a scholarly integrity violation, and offers a disclosure template.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Generative AI is not a source as defined in this provision because its output is not created by a person. If generative AI is permitted by the instructor, students must disclose its use rather than cite or acknowledge the use, since it is an algorithm rather than a source.

All the tenets of scholarly integrity apply to use of generative AI: students must not pass off any output by generative AI as their own, and so a failure of disclosure, even in a course where generative AI is permitted, is a scholarly integrity violation.

newClaim.claimText: Princeton's Rights, Rules, Responsibilities states that students must adhere to course and departmental generative AI policies, and that inappropriate uses on work submitted for an academic requirement - directly copying output, representing AI output as their own (including rewording or paraphrasing it), exceeding the instructor's parameters, or failing to disclose use (including use for rewording, paraphrasing or editing) - constitute academic integrity violations.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Students are responsible for adhering to course and departmental policies regarding the use of generative AI. Inappropriate uses of generative AI on any work submitted to fulfill an academic requirement, such as directly copying the output, representing output generated by or derived from generative AI as their own (including rewording or paraphrasing output from generative AI and representing it as their own), exceeding the parameters of use specified by the instructor, or failing to disclose its use (including the use of generative AI for rewording, paraphrasing or editing) constitute violations of academic integrity.

newEvidence.evidenceSnippet: Students are responsible for adhering to course and departmental policies regarding the use of generative AI. Inappropriate uses of generative AI on any work submitted to fulfill an academic requirement, such as directly copying the output, representing output generated by or derived from generative AI as their own (including rewording or paraphrasing output from generative AI and representing it as their own), exceeding the parameters of use specified by the instructor, or failing to disclose its use (including the use of generative AI for rewording, paraphrasing or editing) constitute violations of academic integrity.

oldClaim.claimText: Princeton University states that inappropriate uses of generative AI on any work submitted to fulfill an academic requirement, including directly copying the output, representing output as the student's own, exceeding instructor parameters, or failing to disclose its use, would constitute violations of academic integrity (Rights, Rules, Responsibilities section 2.4.6).

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Students are responsible for familiarizing themselves with and adhering to course and departmental policies regarding the use of generative AI. newClaim.claimText: Princeton's Generative AI Tools Use Policy (last updated August 2026) governs Princeton administrative and operational information, including student, financial and HR information; it expressly excludes information used for research, academic or instructional purposes. Under it, only University-licensed generative AI tools should be used with University Information classified as Internal or Confidential, publicly available generative AI tools may not be used with such information, and even University-licensed tools should not be used with Restricted information. It is not a blanket rule covering all student coursework or research data.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: The purpose of this policy is to manage the use of Princeton University administrative and operational information with generative AI tools.
For the purposes of this policy, University Information does not include information used for research, academic or instructional purposes.
University-licensed generative AI tools should be used with Princeton Information classified as Internal or Confidential under the University’s Information Security Policy

The use of publicly available generative AI tools in conjunction with such Princeton Information is not permitted by the University. University-licensed generative AI tools should not be used with Princeton Information classified as Restricted.

newClaim.claimText: Princeton's Department of Art and Archaeology prohibits using AI as a text-generation tool in coursework, final examinations and independent projects: students may not submit AI-generated text, use AI-generated text as a draft they then modify or paraphrase, or use generative AI to edit and revise their work. Instructors may grant exceptions for a course assignment with written disclosure, but exceptions will never be made for the junior paper or senior thesis. This department rule is stricter than general course-by-course permission.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: As a result, the Department of Art & Archaeology explicitly prohibits the use of AI as a text-generation tool in the writing of coursework, final examinations, and independent projects alike.

A student may not rely on AI-generated text as a rough or partial draft, which they then modify or paraphrase before submitting it as their own work; likewise, a student may not use generative AI in editing and revising their work.

That said, an instructor may wish to grant exceptions for AI use in a course assignment as long as the student strictly follows the instructor’s guidelines and discloses the specific use in writing. Exceptions will never be made for the junior paper or the senior thesis.

newClaim.claimText: University of Sydney academic decisions and misconduct findings use different review routes. For academic decisions, students may apply for faculty or Academic Panel review within 20 working days, and may appeal to the Student Appeals Body (SAB) within 15 working days of the review outcome, but not simply because they disagree with it. Where the Registrar makes a misconduct finding or penalty, the student may appeal to the Student Disciplinary Appeals Committee (SDAC) within 20 working days of the penalty notice. Not every AI-related academic integrity matter is a Registrar misconduct decision.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
If an informal resolution doesn’t resolve your concerns, the next level available to you is to apply for a review from the relevant faculty or administrative unit.
You must apply within 20 working days of receiving:

If you apply for a SAB appeal, you must apply within 15 working days of receiving the outcome of your faculty or Academic Panel review. If you are granted an extension, you must apply within the extended timeframe.
You cannot appeal to the SAB simply because you disagree with the faculty or Academic Panel review outcome.
To be eligible for a disciplinary appeal, you will need to submit your appeal within 20 working days of receiving your penalty notice from the Registrar.

newClaim.claimText: Higher degree by research (HDR) students at the University of Sydney do not inherit the open-assessment AI permission. The Graduate Research guidance says generative AI may in general be used to improve spelling or grammar (spelling/grammar checkers and reference managers are permitted) but not to generate content; prompting AI to generate written or other content, uploading a draft to improve its academic language, and incorporating AI outputs as substantive thesis content are prohibited, except where AI is integral to the research design or methodology and approved by the supervisor and through the ethics arrangements. HDR students should never enter personal, sensitive or confidential information into any gen AI tool.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: In general terms, gen AI tools may be used where, for example, they assist in improving the spelling or grammar of your writing, but not where they generate content for you.

However, inputting prompts into a gen AI tool (e.g. Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, etc.) to generate written or other content; uploading a draft of your work into a gen AI tool to improve the academic language or any other aspect of your work; and/or incorporating gen AI outputs as substantive content in your thesis or other submitted work are all prohibited, except under certain circumstances as outlined under ‘Responsible use of generative AI in research’.
The responsible use of gen AI tools may be permitted when it is integral to your research design or methodology and its use has been approved by your supervisor.

If you are considering using any form of gen AI or gen AI-assisted technology as part of your research methodology or in ways integral to your research project, you must check with your supervisor first to confirm whether this is permitted.  Then it should be approved as part of your ethics arrangements.
Never enter or upload any personal, sensitive or confidential information into any gen AI tool.

newClaim.claimText: University of Sydney guidance states that misusing AI can breach the Academic Integrity Policy, with examples including submitting AI-generated work without appropriate acknowledgment, using AI where it has been prohibited in a secure assessment such as a secure exam, and inputting University teaching or course materials, other students' content, external partners' intellectual property or any person's personal or health information. Citing non-existent references because AI output was not verified is not acceptable and risks an academic integrity breach.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
Misusing AI can breach the Academic Integrity Policy. Examples of misuse include:
Submitting AI-generated work without appropriate acknowledgment
using AI where it has been prohibited in a ‘secure’ assessment type, such as during a secure exam
inputting University teaching or course materials, content generated by another student, intellectual property from external partners, or any person’s personal or health information.
Citing references that do not exist because you failed to verify AI outputs is not acceptable and puts you at risk of an academic integrity breach, alongside the likely loss of marks.

newClaim.claimText: If University of Sydney students use AI in assessments they must acknowledge it, including generative AI translation, paraphrasing or referencing tools; tools used only for word processing or basic spelling and grammar correction need not be acknowledged. Where permitted by the unit outline, the statement must say that AI tools were used and give the tool's name and version, the publisher, the URL and a brief description of how it was used; unit coordinators may add requirements such as a log of AI inputs and outputs.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: If you use AI in your assessments, you're required to acknowledge it – this includes acknowledging any tools that use generative AI, such as translation tools, paraphrasing tools or referencing tools. You are not required to acknowledge tools used for word processing, or which only correct basic spelling and grammar.

If you're permitted to use automated writing tools or generative AI as per the unit outline, you will need to include a statement in your submitted work explaining:
that you have used AI tools in completing the work
the name and version of the automated writing or generative AI tools you have used
the publisher
the uniform resource locator (URL)
and a brief description of how you have used them.

If your unit coordinator has made any additional stipulations about how they want the class to acknowledge AI use, you should also follow these rules. For example, they may require you to submit a log of the AI inputs and outputs used during the preparation of your assessment.

newClaim.claimText: The AI charter of CIENS (an interdisciplinary centre of ENS-PSL) applies to CIENS students, teachers and researchers only. It allows generative AI as occasional help for translation, document exploration, exploratory document analysis or organising work, but prohibits producing false references, developing a research problem and scientific reasoning, writing the text content, and giving AI sensitive, protected or confidential information. Any AI use must be stated in a note or the body of the text, naming the tool and the nature of use; undeclared use may be treated as academic fraud and lead to disciplinary sanctions. These are unit-level rules, not PSL-wide rules.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Cette charte vise à encadrer l’utilisation des IAg de manière éthique, responsable et durable pour les étudiants du CIENS mais aussi ses enseignants et ses chercheurs.

Ces outils peuvent constituer une aide ponctuelle dans certaines étapes du travail telles que la traduction, l’exploration documentaire, l’analyse exploratoire de documents ou encore l’organisation du travail. Cependant, ils ne se substituent en aucun cas à l’effort intellectuel et à la réflexion personnelle qui doivent être fournis.

Production de fausses références
Élaborer une problématique et un raisonnement scientifique
Rédiger le contenu textuel
Fournir à l’IAg des informations sensibles, protégées et confidentielles.

Tout recours à un outil d’intelligence artificielle doit être mentionné par une note ou dans le corps du texte ; l’outil utilisé ainsi que la nature de l’usage qui en a été fait doivent être précisés.
L’usage non déclaré de l’IAG est susceptible d’être considéré comme une fraude académique. Des sanctions disciplinaires peuvent être appliquées.

newClaim.claimText: PSL's Charte du doctorat (June 2026, section 2.7) sets general recommendations on generative AI for doctoral candidates, some of which are mandatory. Generative AI is not prohibited in doctoral research, but its uses must be transparent, declared and critically assessed, and the candidate remains fully responsible for AI-obtained content. Candidates must insert a dated, signed 'Déclaration doctorale d'intégrité scientifique' (one to two pages) at the start of the thesis, stating which generative AI tools were used, for which tasks, their benefits, limits and risks, and any mitigation. Member institutions may set stricter rules, which prevail.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: L’Université PSL formule un cadre de recommandations générales relatives aux usages de l’intelligence artificielle générative (I.A.G.) dont certaines dispositions sont obligatoires pour les étudiants réalisant leur doctorat dans cette Université.

Il s’ensuit que l’utilisation de l’I.A.G. n’est pas interdite dans le contexte d’une recherche doctorale, mais les usages, à l’instar d’autres outils, doivent être transparents, déclarés et faire l’objet d’un retour critique de la part du doctorant.
Les établissements-composantes sont susceptibles de définir des règles plus précises en matière d'I.A.G., qui prévaudront.

Cette déclaration doit être datée et signée par le doctorant et insérée dans les premières pages du manuscrit de doctorat.

newClaim.claimText: Université PSL's Règlement de la scolarité for 2026-2027 (adopted by the Board on 25 June 2026, replacing the June 2025 version with the same AI wording) states that, where an instructor authorises AI-based tools such as ChatGPT, their use must be explicitly disclosed like any source citation, and failure to disclose AI use is treated as plagiarism and sanctioned as such; a disciplinary procedure may follow, with sanctions up to exclusion (not automatic exclusion). The 2026 version applies to programmes operated directly by PSL (such as the Collège Sciences, Humanités et Société and the Paris School of AI); member institutions apply their own regulations, so it does not set course permissions across ENS, Dauphine, Mines Paris and other members.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Le présent règlement s'applique aux formations directement opérées par l'Université PSL (Collège Sciences, Humanités et Société, Paris School of AI, …).

Lorsque celui-ci est autorisé par l’enseignante ou l’enseignant, le recours à des outils basés sur l’intelligence artificielle (IA), tels que ChatGPT, doit être signalé explicitement (de la même manière que toute référence ou citation de source). Ne pas signaler l’utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle est considéré comme un acte de plagiat et sera sanctionné comme tel.

En cas de soupçon de plagiat, l’enseignante ou l’enseignant doit informer l’équipe de direction et lui communiquer tous les éléments à disposition. Une procédure disciplinaire peut être déclenchée avec une sanction pouvant aller jusqu’à l’exclusion.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: La reproductibilité de la recherche est un principe de base de l’intégrité scientifique. Or ce principe est mis à mal par l’utilisation de l’IA. newClaim.claimText: Where approved generative AI use contributes to a University of Toronto doctoral thesis, the thesis must appropriately cite and describe that use so the reader can tell which tools were used, and how and why. Approval to use AI in research does not extend to writing: graduate students must separately seek and document supervisor and committee approval for AI use in writing. SGS does not regulate master's theses, Major Research Papers or comprehensive exams; graduate units set those rules, while the Code of Behaviour and research-misconduct framework still apply.
newClaim.claimValue: University of Toronto graduate students must clearly describe and cite any generative AI tools used in thesis research or writing.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Careful attention must be paid in the thesis to appropriately citing and describing any use of generative AI tools in the research process. It must be clear to the reader which generative AI tools were used, as well as how and why they were used.

Graduate students must seek and document approval from their supervisors and committees for the use of generative AI in writing even if they already have approval to use generative AI tools in their research.

SGS does not regulate master’s-level theses, Major Research Papers, or qualifying / comprehensive exams. However, SGS recommends that graduate units make use of the principles outlined for doctoral-level work in articulating requirements for any master’s-level research-based works.

newClaim.claimText: The University of Toronto does not support the use of AI-detection software on student work, because none has been found sufficiently reliable and sharing student work with such programs without permission raises privacy and ethical concerns. Instructors are encouraged to use traditional methods instead, such as meeting with the student to discuss their work.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: The University does not support the use of AI-detection software programs on student work. None of these software programs have been found to be sufficiently reliable, and they are known to incorrectly flag instances of AI use in human-written content.

However, instructors are encouraged to continue to use their traditional methods for detection of potential academic misconduct, including meeting with a student to discuss their work in person, using short in-person assessments that ask students to expand on the ideas in their out-of-class assignments, and so on.

newClaim.claimText: The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

newClaim.claimText: The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Undergraduate and graduate students may use GenAI tools as learning aids, for example, to summarize information or test their understanding of a topic. These tools should be used in a manner similar to consulting library books, online sources, peers, or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has stated that AI tools are not otherwise permitted in the course. These uses typically do not need to be cited or disclosed.

However, if students use information from GenAI tools that would normally require citation (e.g., quoting, paraphrasing, or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite their use according to guidelines provided by U of T Libraries or as directed by their instructor.

newClaim.claimText: University of Toronto CTSI guidance on using non-supported (unvetted) AI tools in courses says students must be able to opt out: instructors cannot require students to accept a third party's terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property, and must provide a viable alternative where the tool is part of a required activity or assessment. A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Students must be able to opt out. You cannot require students to accept a third party’s terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property. If the tool is part of a required activity or assessment, you must provide a viable alternative for students who decline.

A Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) is required wherever personally identifying information is collected. Under U of T’s FIPPA obligations, any unvetted tool that collects personal information (e.g., student names, email addresses, assessment submissions) needs a PIA to be conducted. This process typically takes four to eight weeks from the time all required information has been received.

newClaim.claimText: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. If an instructor has specified that no outside assistance is permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider the student's use of generative AI to be use of an unauthorized aid. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: to use or possess an unauthorized aid or aids or obtain or provide unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work;

if an instructor specified that no outside assistance was permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider a student’s use of generative AI to be use of an “unauthorized aid” under the Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters.
If your instructor advised you that use of AI tools was prohibited, using a generative AI tool to create even part of your marked assignment would be considered use of an unauthorized aid.

newClaim.claimText: University of Toronto teaching guidance (CTSI) now names Cogniti as the preferred tool for teaching and learning, embedded in Quercus and free for every student, and Microsoft Copilot Chat as the easiest general-purpose starting point available to everyone at U of T. Tools in the AI Kitchen are vetted and may be used with institutional data up to Level 3. Some licensed tools require a paid subscription not covered by the University. Tool availability does not authorize AI use in a given assessment.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Cogniti is the preferred tool for teaching and learning. It is built for education: embedded in Quercus, free for every student, highly customizable, and can be grounded in your course content.
Microsoft Copilot Chat is the easiest place to start. It is a general-purpose tool available to everyone at U of T and is the lowest-barrier way for students to build basic AI literacy.

Licensed Tools in the AI Kitchen (such as Claude for Education, ChatGPT Edu and M365 Copilot) may suit your own course preparation and other projects where advanced features can add value. However, some of these tools require a paid subscription that is not covered by the University.

Tools in the AI Kitchen are vetted for privacy and security and covered by U of T’s data protection standards: your prompts and your students’ data are never used to train AI models, and you can use institutional data up to Level 3, such as course materials and student assessments.

newClaim.claimText: On 12 January 2026 Fudan launched the AI3A education co-creation platform and published the Generative AI Education and Teaching Application Guide 1.0, with 11 annexes such as an AI use declaration template and reference syllabus clauses. According to Fudan's official announcement, the guide allows AI for supporting steps such as language polishing and structural suggestions but not to replace core academic work such as research conception, theory building and data analysis, and judges integrity mainly on honest disclosure and process records. The guide's full text sits on the AI3A platform and was not independently reviewed; it is teaching guidance and does not by itself override the stricter undergraduate-thesis rule.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: 1月12日，复旦大学正式上线AI3A教育共创平台，同步发布《复旦大学生成式人工智能教育教学应用指引1.0版》
它明确，AI可用于语言润色、结构建议等辅助环节，但不得替代研究构思、理论构建、数据分析等核心学术劳动。判定依据则侧重于学生是否如实披露、是否有过程记录可供核查，以及教师是否通过课程要求、答辩等方式进行了合理性验证。
而《应用指引》更是一个“拿来即用”的工具包，附有11个可操作的附件，涵盖教学设计模板、伦理声明范例、课堂协议等，真正让师生用好、用对AI。

newClaim.claimText: Under Fudan's Student Disciplinary Regulations (2017, amended 2019), students must be informed of their right to state their case and defend themselves before a sanction. A student who disagrees with a disciplinary decision may appeal to the University Student Appeals Committee within ten days (not working days) of service of the decision; the committee normally concludes within fifteen days (extendable by fifteen), and a student who disagrees with the review decision may appeal to the Shanghai Municipal Education Commission within fifteen days of its service (Student Appeals Regulations, effective 1 September 2017). A teacher's request to redo or supplement an assessment is not automatically a disciplinary decision.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: 第十六条 学生本人不服处分决定的，可以在处分决定书送达之日起十日内向学校学生申诉处理委员会提出申诉。
学生提出申诉，应当在处理决定书送达之日起十日内，向学生申诉处理委员会递交申诉申请书，并提供处理决定书的副本。
学生申诉处理委员会对申诉案件，应当在收到申诉申请书之日起十五日内作出复查结论并告知申诉人。有特殊情况需要延长的，由学生申诉处理委员会主任批准，可以延长十五日。
申诉人对复查决定有异议的，在复查决定书送达之日起十五日内，可以向上海市教育委员会提出申诉。

newClaim.claimText: Under the Fudan undergraduate-thesis AI rule, breaches are handled according to their seriousness: they may be reflected in the thesis assessment grade, lead to refusal of the defence or cancellation of a passing grade, and only where they constitute academic misconduct lead to disciplinary sanctions, loss of degree eligibility or degree revocation. Course papers, term papers and exam papers may refer to this rule where no specific rule exists, while published academic papers and research activities are governed by other rules and are outside its scope. Supervisors and reviewers may add supplementary assessment to check the student's mastery.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: 学生违反相关规定使用 AI 工具的，视情节给予纳入本科毕业论文（设计）考核成绩、不准答辩、取消合格成绩等处理；构成学术不端（不当）的，按照相关校纪校规给予纪律处分、取消学位申请资格、撤销学位等处理。
考试论文、学年论文、课程论文等考核性论文（设计）若无具体的针对性规定，亦可参照此规定执行。
在发表的学术论文（交流性论文）或学术研究活动中使用 AI 工具另有规定，不适用此规定。
11月28日，复旦发布《复旦大学关于在本科毕业论文（设计）中使用AI工具的规定（试行）》（以下简称《规定》），对AI工具的使用进行详细规范。

newClaim.claimText: When AI tools are used in a Fudan undergraduate thesis, the thesis commitment form must disclose the tool name and version, time and specific purpose of use, the content or suggestions the AI produced, and the parts of the thesis where it was used; students must keep the relevant pre-AI materials for inspection by the supervisor or reviewers. The author bears final responsibility and AI cannot be listed as an author.

须保留 AI 工具处理之前的相关重要材料，以备指导老师或评审专家对学生使用 AI 工具的检查和质询。

newClaim.claimText: The same Fudan undergraduate-thesis rule (Article 4) prohibits AI in six areas: research design and data analysis; generating or altering original data (unless AI itself is the research topic); generating or altering original result images and key illustrations (unless a reproducible AI method is part of the design and explained in the methods); directly generating thesis text or acknowledgements, including AI language polishing and translation; use of AI by defence committee members or reviewers to evaluate the thesis; and any AI use or upload for theses involving confidential content.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: 研究设计与数据分析：禁止使用 AI 工具进行研究方案设计、创新性方法设计、算法（模型）框架搭建、毕业论文（设计）结构设计、研究（设计）选题、研究（设计）意义及创新性总结、研究假设提出、数据分析、结果分析与讨论和结论总结等。
原始数据收集：禁止使用 AI 工具生成或改动本科毕业论文（设计）中的原始数据，如实验数据、统计数据、田野调查数据等。
语言表达能力仍然是毕业论文（设计）考察的重点，禁止使用 AI 工具进行语言润色和翻译。
答辩与检查：答辩或校内论文检查时，禁止答辩委员、评审专家使用任何 AI 工具对学生的本科毕业论文（设计）进行评审
涉密内容：本科毕业论文（设计）涉及保密内容的，禁止使用任何 AI 工具，禁止上传任何数据和图片到 AI 平台。

newClaim.claimText: Fudan's formal rule on AI tools in undergraduate theses (adopted by the Academic Affairs Office on 24 September 2024, trial) allows AI use only with the supervisor's consent and only where AI output does not affect assessment of the student's own innovative ability, in four areas: literature search and management (verifying references), suggesting chart types and auxiliary charting (not generating or altering original data or key research figures), coding and method screening where the method is not the thesis's innovation (all code and methods must be reviewed and tested by the author), and reference formatting (with checking). This rule is specific to undergraduate theses; it is not a rule for all courses or for graduate theses.
newClaim.claimValue: Fudan Student Affairs Office states, by reference to Fudan undergraduate-thesis AI tool rules, that AI assistance in undergraduate thesis writing requires teacher consent and disclosure, core innovative work must not rely on AI, and confidential or private content must not be used with AI.

newClaim.claimText: King's Academic Misconduct Policy states that using generative AI tools to produce output that is then copied as part of a submission is not appropriate, that any work submitted must genuinely demonstrate the student's own work, skills and knowledge and follow the assessment guidelines, and that generative AI writing programmes are third-party technologies to be used only in accordance with College guidance. The King's guidance adds that submitting AI-generated text as one's own without written departmental permission is considered misconduct (third-party involvement or text manipulation) where it gives undue advantage or interferes with assessment of the student's own understanding. A written permission or acknowledgement does not by itself make substantive AI content creation acceptable.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: However, the use of generative AI tools to produce output which is then copied as part of a submission is not appropriate. Prudent, ethical and constructive use of tools is increasingly likely to form part of the production of assessed work.

This means that any work submitted must represent a genuine demonstration of the student’s own work, skills and subject knowledge, adheres to the guidelines of the assessment task, and respects the College’s value of academic integrity and honesty.
The service should not assist with substantive content creation or structuring of the assessment. Above all, third parties cannot make substantive changes which compromise the authorship of the text
For the avoidance of doubt, generative Artificial Intelligence writing programmes are third party technologies and must only be used in accordance with College guidance.

Submitting text generated by technology/artificial intelligence as their own, without written permission from their department is considered misconduct under the offences of third-party involvement or text manipulation, if it provides undue advantage or interferes with assessment of the student's own understanding.

newClaim.claimText: King's College London permits doctoral students to use generative AI tools in an assistive role in thesis writing, to clarify their own writing and avoid misrepresenting their meaning; this can include rewriting, rephrasing or paraphrasing parts of the thesis. Use beyond the circumstances permitted by the doctoral guidance risks breaching the Academic Misconduct Policy, and AI used in the research process itself (for example to analyse data) is largely outside this guidance and falls under research design, ethical review and research-integrity norms.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Yes, students are permitted to make use of generative AI tools in their thesis writing processes. However, where a student's use of generative AI tools in their thesis writing exceeds the circumstances permitted by this guidance, they will risk breaching the Academic Misconduct Policy.

Doctoral students can use generative AI tools in an assistive role to clarify their own writing and help ensure that their own meaning is not misrepresented due to the quality and standard of the English used. This may go beyond simply correcting spelling and basic grammar, and can involve the rewriting, rephrasing and/or paraphrasing parts of the thesis.

The use of AI tools as part of the research process – to analyse and draw insights from data, for example – is therefore largely beyond the scope of this guidance. At a minimum, such usage would, like any other element of research design, be clearly outlined by authors in a ‘Methods’ section, subject to ethical review where appropriate, and conducted in accordance with principles of research integrity as well as disciplinary norms.

newClaim.claimText: King's College London suggests four broad levels of generative AI use in assessment that programme and module leaders may adjust to each assessment: Minimal (routine tools such as auto transcription, spell and grammar checkers), Limited/selective (clearly delineated tasks as allowed), Open (no specific restrictions but key stages and tools must be tracked) and Embedded (AI use is a focal part of the assessment). The levels are a framework for the actual assessment brief, not an automatic university-wide permission, and verbatim use of generated content without acknowledgement is never appropriate.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: We have suggested four broad levels that your Programme and Module leaders may adjust to the specifics of an assessment:
Includes routine and established use of tools such as auto transcription, spell checkers, grammar check.
Use for clearly delineated tasks as appropriate/allowed/recommended.
No specific restrictions but with requirement to track key stages/tools utilised.
AI use is a feature of the assessment itself. Here the use of generative AI is a focal aspect of the assessment.

Once again, we state that in no circumstance is it appropriate to use generated content verbatim without clear indication and acknowledgement, or to effectively outsource the writing task as much as it is inappropriate to get someone else to write something and claim it as your own.

newClaim.claimText: Under King's Academic Misconduct Policy, a suspected case normally goes first to a Stage One Academic Integrity Meeting (AIM) with two staff members. The AIM is not a hearing and should be informal, supportive and exploratory; where authorship or third-party involvement is in doubt the student may be asked to explain their answers, ideas or references, but must not be pressured or obliged to give specific responses and may respond in writing instead. Staff share their notes, and the student may add information, normally within 5 working days. Possible Stage One outcomes are no concern, poor academic practice, a local educative or restorative outcome, or referral to a Stage Two Misconduct Committee.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: The student will be invited to attend the Academic Integrity Meeting (AIM), which will normally be with any two of the following staff members: module leader, programme leader (or deputy), ASB Chair (or nominee), Programme Manager or personal tutor.
The meeting is not a hearing, and the meeting should be informal, supportive and exploratory.

Where the academic integrity concerns involve concerns of third-party involvement or doubts about the authorship of the submission, it is appropriate to ask the student to explain their answers, ideas, concepts or references.
The student should not be under any pressure, or obliged to provide specific responses. If a student declines to engage with the AIM, they will have the opportunity to provide a written response.

Staff should keep notes of the discussion and share these with the student, along with any other relevant materials discussed (e.g. items listed in 7.3). The student may provide any other relevant information after the meeting, and should normally do this within 5 working days.
4. That the matter should be referred to Stage Two.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: When postgraduate research students submit their thesis to the Research Degrees team, they are also required to submit a completed “Thesis Submission Declaration Form (RD2)” signed by the student and their supervisors. I declare that no part of this thesis has been generated by AI software. These are my own words, and all references are cited accordingly.

I declare that my use of AI software is consistent with the research degree award criteria outlined in the Framework for Postgraduate Research Awards. Please note that both of these declarations describe permitted approaches to thesis authorship for King’s research degrees.

newClaim.claimText: King's Academic Misconduct Policy provides two different review routes with different start points. Where a Stage One AIM finds misconduct and applies a local penalty (Outcome 3), the student may send a contestation in writing to Student Conduct & Appeals within 10 working days from the date of written notification of the Stage One outcome. A Stage Two Misconduct Committee decision may be appealed, on the grounds of new evidence or significant procedural error, by submitting a Misconduct Appeal Form within 10 working days of the date of the Misconduct Committee outcome. Possible outcomes range from educative measures such as a formal warning or capped resubmission to punitive outcomes up to suspension or expulsion; AI use does not carry an automatic penalty.

newClaim.claimText: King's Academic Misconduct Policy distinguishes poor academic practice from academic misconduct: an ASB Chair may decide a concern is an unintentional misunderstanding of scholarly practice (for example incomplete citation), which is not misconduct; the student receives feedback and the work is marked against the criteria. Blatant, extensive or careless failures are excluded from this category.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Once the ASB Chair (or their nominee) has reviewed the information available, they may decide that the concern relates to poor academic practice and that no academic misconduct has occurred. Poor academic practice involves an unintentional misunderstanding of scholarly practice. Examples include when sources are acknowledged to some extent, but citation is inadequate or incomplete. It does not include when the failure to adhere to scholarly practice is blatant, extensive or results from a lack of effort. Poor academic practice is not a form of academic misconduct.
